danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 19
paragraphs: Den fireogtyvende august fandt slaget ved Sjevardino-redouten sted, den femogtyvende faldt ikke et eneste skud fra nogen af siderne, og den seksogtyvende udkæmpedes selve slaget ved Borodino.

Hvorfor og hvordan blev slagene ved Sjevardino og Borodino givet og modtaget? Hvorfor blev slaget ved Borodino udkæmpet? Der var ikke den mindste mening i det, hverken for franskmændene eller russerne. Dets umiddelbare resultat for russerne var, og måtte nødvendigvis være, at vi blev bragt nærmere Moskvas ødelæggelse — som vi frygtede mere end noget andet i verden; og for franskmændene var dets umiddelbare resultat, at de blev bragt nærmere tilintetgørelsen af hele deres hær — som de frygtede mere end noget andet i verden. Hvad resultatet måtte blive, var ganske indlysende, og dog tilbød Napoleon og Kutuzov accepterede det slag.

Hvis hærførerne havde ladet sig lede af fornuften, måtte det have stået klart for Napoleon, at han ved at rykke tretten hundrede mil frem og give slag med sandsynlighed for at miste en fjerdedel af sin hær marcherede mod sin sikre undergang, og det måtte have været lige så klart for Kutuzov, at han ved at acceptere slaget og risikere at miste en fjerdedel af sin hær med sikkerhed ville miste Moskva. For Kutuzov var dette matematisk klart, ligesom det er klart, at hvis jeg i damspil har én brik færre og bliver ved med at bytte, taber jeg med sikkerhed, og derfor ikke bør bytte. Når min modstander har seksten brikker, og jeg har fjorten, er jeg kun en ottendedel svagere, men når jeg har byttet tretten brikker mere, er han tre gange så stærk som jeg.

Før slaget ved Borodino stod vores styrke i forhold til franskmændenes omtrent som fem til seks, men efter det slag som lidt mere end én til to: før havde vi hundrede tusind mod hundrede og tyve tusind, bagefter lidt over halvtreds tusind mod hundrede tusind. Og dog tog den erfarne og skarpsindige Kutuzov imod slaget, mens Napoleon, der blev kaldt et militært geni, gav det og mistede en fjerdedel af sin hær og forlængede sine forsyningslinjer yderligere. Hvis man siger, at han ventede at afslutte krigen ved at indtage Moskva, ligesom han havde afsluttet et tidligere felttog ved at indtage Wien, taler meget imod dette. Napoleons egne historikere fortæller os, at han fra Smolensk og fremad ønskede at standse, vidste faren ved sin udstrakte stilling, og vidste, at indtagelsen af Moskva ikke ville betyde felttogets afslutning, for han havde set i Smolensk, i hvilken tilstand de russiske byer blev overladt til ham, og ikke havde modtaget et eneste svar på sine gentagne meddelelser om sit ønske om at forhandle.

Da Kutuzov gav og modtog slag ved Borodino, handlede han ufrivilligt og irrationelt. Men bagefter, for at tilpasse det skete, fremlagde historikerne snedigt udtænkte beviser på forudseen og genialitet hos de generaler, der af alle historiens blinde redskaber var de mest bundne og ufrivillige.

De gamle har efterladt os forbilledlige heltedigte, hvori heltene udgør hele historiens interesse, og vi er stadig ude af stand til at vænne os til den kendsgerning, at historier af den art for vores epoke er meningsløse.

Om det andet spørgsmål — hvordan slagene ved Borodino og det forudgående slag ved Sjevardino blev udkæmpet — hersker der ligeledes en bestemt og velkendt, men ganske fejlagtig opfattelse. Alle historikere beskriver sagen som følger:
Den russiske hær, siger de, søgte under sin tilbagetrækning fra Smolensk den bedste stilling til et generalslag og fandt en sådan stilling ved Borodino.
Russerne, siger de, befæstede denne stilling på forhånd til venstre for landevejen (fra Moskva til Smolensk) og næsten vinkelret på den, fra Borodino til Utitsa, netop dér, hvor slaget fandt sted.

Foran denne stilling, hedder det, blev en befæstet forpost oprettet på Sjevardino-højen for at observere fjenden. Den fireogtyvende, fortælles det, angreb Napoleon denne forpost og tog den, og den seksogtyvende angreb han hele den russiske hær, der stod opstillet på Borodino-sletten.
Sådan siger historierne, og det hele er fuldstændig forkert, som enhver, der gider undersøge sagen, let kan overbevise sig om.

Russerne søgte ikke den bedste stilling, men passerede tværtimod under tilbagetrækningen mange stillinger, der var bedre end Borodino. De standsede ikke ved nogen af dem, fordi Kutuzov ikke ønskede at besætte en stilling, han ikke selv havde valgt, fordi det folkelige krav om et slag endnu ikke var kommet stærkt nok til udtryk, og fordi Miloradovitj endnu ikke var ankommet med militsen, og af mange andre grunde. Faktum er, at de andre stillinger, de var passeret, var stærkere, og at stillingen ved Borodino (dér, hvor slaget stod) langtfra var stærk — den var ikke mere en stilling end et hvilket som helst andet punkt i det russiske rige, man kunne finde ved tilfældigt at stikke en nål i et kort.

Ikke alene befæstede russerne ikke stillingen på Borodino-sletten til venstre for og vinkelret på landevejen (altså den stilling, hvor slaget fandt sted), men før den femogtyvende august 1812 tænkte de aldrig på, at et slag kunne komme til at stå dér. Dette fremgik for det første af, at der den femogtyvende ikke var nogen forskansninger, og at dem, der blev påbegyndt den femogtyvende og seksogtyvende, ikke blev færdige, og for det andet af Sjevardino-redoutens placering. Denne redout var ganske meningsløs foran den stilling, hvor slaget blev udkæmpet. Hvorfor var den stærkere befæstet end nogen anden post? Og hvorfor blev alle kræfter opbrugt og seks tusind mand ofret for at forsvare den til langt ud på natten den fireogtyvende? En kosakpatrulje ville have været nok til at observere fjenden. For det tredje — som bevis for, at den stilling, hvor slaget stod, ikke var forudset, og at Sjevardino-redouten ikke var en forpost for den stilling — har vi den kendsgerning, at Barclay de Tolly og Bagration indtil den femogtyvende var overbeviste om, at Sjevardino-redouten var stillingens venstre fløj, og at Kutuzov selv i sin rapport, skrevet i al hast efter slaget, omtaler Sjevardino-redouten som stillingens venstre fløj. Det var meget senere, da rapporterne om slaget ved Borodino blev skrevet i ro og mag, at den fejlagtige og besynderlige påstand blev opfundet (sandsynligvis for at retfærdiggøre en øverstbefalendes fejl, der måtte fremstilles som ufejlbarlig) at Sjevardino-redouten var en forpost — mens den i virkeligheden simpelthen var et befæstet punkt på venstre fløj — og at slaget ved Borodino blev udkæmpet på en på forhånd valgt, forskanset stilling, skønt det faktisk fandt sted på et ganske uventet og næsten ubefæstet sted.

Sagen var tydeligvis denne: en stilling var udvalgt langs floden Kolotja — der krydser landevejen ikke vinkelret, men i en spids vinkel — således at venstre fløj var ved Sjevardino, højre fløj nær landsbyen Novoje, og centrum ved Borodino, hvor floderne Kolotja og Vojna løber sammen.

For enhver, der betragter Borodino-sletten uden at tænke på, hvordan slaget faktisk forløb, fremstår denne stilling, beskyttet af floden Kolotja, som indlysende for en hær, hvis mål var at forhindre fjenden i at rykke frem langs Smolensk-vejen mod Moskva.

Napoleon, der red til Valuevo den fireogtyvende, så ikke (som historiebøgerne hævder) russernes stilling fra Utitsa til Borodino (han kunne ikke have set den stilling, for den fandtes ikke), og han så heller ikke en forpost for den russiske hær, men mens han forfulgte den russiske bagtrop, stødte han på den russiske stillings venstre fløj — ved Sjevardino-redouten — og førte uventet for russerne sin hær over Kolotja. Og russerne, der ikke nåede at indlede et generalslag, trak deres venstre fløj tilbage fra den stilling, de havde tænkt at besætte, og indtog en ny stilling, der hverken var forudset eller befæstet. Ved at krydse Kolotja til venstre for landevejen forskød Napoleon hele det forestående slag fra højre til venstre (set fra russisk side) og overførte det til sletten mellem Utitsa, Semjonovsk og Borodino — en slette, der ikke var mere fordelagtig som stilling end nogen anden slette i Rusland — og dér fandt hele slaget den seksogtyvende august sted.

Hvis Napoleon ikke var redet ud om aftenen den fireogtyvende til Kolotja og ikke da havde beordret et øjeblikkeligt angreb på redouten, men i stedet havde indledt angrebet næste morgen, ville ingen have tvivlet på, at Sjevardino-redouten var vores stillings venstre fløj, og slaget ville have fundet sted, hvor vi ventede det. I så fald ville vi formentlig have forsvaret Sjevardino-redouten — vores venstre fløj — endnu mere hårdnakket. Vi ville have angrebet Napoleon i centrum eller på højre fløj, og kampen ville have fundet sted den femogtyvende i den stilling, vi havde tiltænkt og befæstet. Men da angrebet på vores venstre fløj fandt sted om aftenen efter bagtroppens tilbagetrækning (det vil sige umiddelbart efter kampen ved Gridnjova), og da de russiske hærførere ikke ønskede eller ikke nåede at indlede et generalslag om aftenen den fireogtyvende, var det første og vigtigste afsnit af slaget ved Borodino allerede tabt den fireogtyvende, og dette førte naturligvis til nederlaget den seksogtyvende.

Efter tabet af Sjevardino-redouten stod vi om morgenen den femogtyvende uden en stilling for vores venstre fløj og var tvunget til at bøje den tilbage og i hast forskanse den, hvor den tilfældigt befandt sig.

Ikke alene blev den russiske hær den seksogtyvende forsvaret af svage, ufærdige forskansninger, men denne stillings ulempe blev forstærket af den kendsgerning, at de russiske hærførere — der ikke fuldt ud havde indset, hvad der var sket, nemlig tabet af vores stilling på venstre fløj og forskydningen af hele det forestående slag fra højre til venstre — fastholdt deres udstrakte stilling fra landsbyen Novoje til Utitsa og følgelig måtte flytte deres styrker fra højre til venstre under selve slaget. Således skete det, at russerne gennem hele slaget kun stillede halvdelen af deres styrker op mod den samlede franske hær, der blev kastet mod vores venstre fløj. (Poniatowskis aktion mod Utitsa og Uvarovs på højre fløj mod franskmændene var handlinger, der lå uden for slagets hovedforløb.) Således blev slaget ved Borodino slet ikke udkæmpet, som det er blevet beskrevet (i et forsøg på at skjule vores hærføreres fejl, selv på bekostning af den hæder, der tilkommer den russiske hær og det russiske folk). Slaget ved Borodino blev ikke udkæmpet på en udvalgt og forskanset stilling med styrker, der kun var lidt svagere end fjendens, men — som følge af tabet af Sjevardino-redouten — på en åben og næsten ubefæstet stilling med styrker, der kun var halvt så talrige som franskmændenes; det vil sige under forhold, hvor det ikke blot var utænkeligt at kæmpe i ti timer og opnå et uafgjort resultat, men utænkeligt at holde en hær fra fuldstændig opløsning og flugt.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: On the twenty-fourth of August the battle of the Shevardino Redoubt was fought; on the twenty-fifth not a shot was fired by either side; and on the twenty-sixth the battle of Borodino itself took place.

Why and how were the battles of Shevardino and Borodino fought and accepted? Why was the battle of Borodino fought? There was not the slightest sense in it for either the French or the Russians. Its immediate result for the Russians was, and was bound to be, that we were brought closer to the destruction of Moscow—which we feared more than anything in the world; and for the French, its immediate result was that they were brought closer to the destruction of their whole army—which they feared more than anything in the world. The outcome was completely obvious, and yet Napoleon offered and Kutuzov accepted the battle.

If the commanders had been guided by reason, it would seem obvious to Napoleon that by advancing thirteen hundred miles and fighting with a probability of losing a quarter of his army, he was marching toward certain destruction; and it would have been equally clear to Kutuzov that by accepting battle and risking the loss of a quarter of his army, he would certainly lose Moscow. For Kutuzov this was mathematically clear, just as it is clear in checkers that if I have one piece less and keep trading, I will certainly lose—and therefore should not trade. When my opponent has sixteen pieces and I have fourteen, I am only one-eighth weaker; but when I have traded away thirteen more, he will be three times as strong as I am.

Before the battle of Borodino our strength relative to the French was about five to six, but after the battle it was little more than one to two: before the battle we had a hundred thousand against a hundred and twenty thousand; afterward, barely fifty thousand against a hundred thousand. Yet the shrewd and experienced Kutuzov accepted the battle, while Napoleon, supposedly a commander of genius, offered it—losing a quarter of his army and stretching his supply lines even further. If we are told he expected to end the campaign by capturing Moscow, as he had ended a previous campaign by capturing Vienna, there is much evidence to the contrary. Napoleon's own historians tell us that from Smolensk onward he wanted to stop, that he knew the danger of his extended position, and that he knew the occupation of Moscow would not end the campaign, for he had seen at Smolensk the state in which Russian towns were being left to him, and had received not a single reply to his repeated proposals to negotiate.

In giving and accepting battle at Borodino, Kutuzov acted involuntarily and irrationally. But later, to fit what had occurred, historians provided cleverly crafted evidence of the foresight and genius of the generals who, of all the blind tools of history, were the most enslaved and involuntary.

The ancients left us model heroic poems in which the heroes supply the entire interest of the story, and we are still unable to accustom ourselves to the fact that for our era, such histories are meaningless.

On the other question—how the battles of Borodino and Shevardino were actually fought—there also exists a definite, well-known, but quite false account. All the historians describe the affair as follows:
The Russian army, they say, in its retreat from Smolensk, sought the best position for a general battle and found it at Borodino.

The Russians, they say, fortified this position in advance on the left of the highway (from Moscow to Smolensk) and almost at right angles to it, from Borodino to Utitsa, at the very place where the battle was fought.

In front of this position, they say, a fortified outpost was established on the Shevardino mound to observe the enemy. On the twenty-fourth, we are told, Napoleon attacked this advanced post and took it, and on the twenty-sixth attacked the whole Russian army, which was in position on the field of Borodino.
So the histories say, and it is all quite wrong, as anyone who cares to examine the matter can easily see.

The Russians did not seek the best position; on the contrary, during the retreat they passed many positions better than Borodino. They did not stop at any of them because Kutuzov did not wish to occupy a position he had not chosen himself, because the popular demand for battle had not yet been expressed strongly enough, because Miloradovich had not yet arrived with the militia, and for many other reasons. The fact is that other positions they had passed were stronger, and the position at Borodino (where the battle was fought), far from being strong, was no more of a position than any other random spot in the Russian Empire.

Not only did the Russians not fortify the position on the field of Borodino to the left of and at right angles to the highway (the position where the battle took place), but never until the twenty-fifth of August, 1812, did they even consider that a battle might be fought there. This is shown, first, by the fact that there were no entrenchments there by the twenty-fifth, and those begun on the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth were never completed; and second, by the position of the Shevardino Redoubt. That redoubt was quite senseless as an outpost of the position where the battle was actually accepted. Why was it more heavily fortified than any other point? And why were all efforts exhausted and six thousand men sacrificed defending it until late at night on the twenty-fourth? A Cossack patrol would have sufficed to observe the enemy. Third, as proof that the position where the battle was fought had not been planned, and that the Shevardino Redoubt was not an advanced post of that position, we have the fact that until the twenty-fifth, both Barclay de Tolly and Bagration believed the Shevardino Redoubt was the left flank of the position, and that Kutuzov himself, in his report written hastily after the battle, calls the Shevardino Redoubt the left flank of the position. It was only much later, when reports on the battle of Borodino were written at leisure, that the incorrect and extraordinary claim was invented (probably to justify the mistakes of a commander in chief who had to be portrayed as infallible) that the Shevardino Redoubt was an advanced post—whereas in reality it was simply a fortified point on the left flank—and that the battle of Borodino was fought on a pre-selected, entrenched position, whereas it was actually fought on a nearly unexpected and almost unfortified spot.

The situation was clearly this: a position was selected along the river Kolocha—which crosses the highway not at a right angle but at an acute angle—so that the left flank was at Shevardino, the right flank near the village of Novoe, and the center at Borodino at the confluence of the Kolocha and Voyna rivers.

To anyone looking at the field of Borodino without considering how the battle was actually fought, this position, protected by the river Kolocha, seems the obvious one for an army trying to prevent an enemy from advancing along the Smolensk road to Moscow.

Napoleon, riding to Valuevo on the twenty-fourth, did not see (as the history books claim) the Russian position from Utitsa to Borodino (he could not have seen that position because it did not exist), nor did he see an advanced post of the Russian army. Instead, while pursuing the Russian rearguard, he came upon the left flank of the Russian position—at the Shevardino Redoubt—and unexpectedly moved his army across the Kolocha. The Russians, not having time to begin a general battle, pulled back their left wing from the position they had intended to hold and took up a new position that had not been planned and was not fortified. By crossing the Kolocha to the left of the highway, Napoleon shifted the entire coming battle from right to left (from the Russian perspective) and transferred it to the plain between Utitsa, Semenovsk, and Borodino—a plain no more advantageous than any other in Russia—and there the entire battle of the twenty-sixth of August took place.

Had Napoleon not ridden out on the evening of the twenty-fourth to the Kolocha, and had he not then ordered an immediate attack on the redoubt but instead begun the attack the next morning, no one would have doubted that the Shevardino Redoubt was the left flank of our position, and the battle would have taken place where we expected. In that case, we would probably have defended the Shevardino Redoubt—our left flank—even more stubbornly. We would have attacked Napoleon in the center or on the right, and the battle would have been fought on the twenty-fifth in the position we had intended and fortified. But since the attack on our left flank came in the evening after the retreat of our rearguard (that is, immediately after the fight at Gridneva), and since the Russian commanders could not or would not begin a general engagement on the evening of the twenty-fourth, the first and decisive action of the battle of Borodino was already lost on the twenty-fourth, and this obviously led to the loss of the one fought on the twenty-sixth.

After the loss of the Shevardino Redoubt, we found ourselves on the morning of the twenty-fifth without a position for our left flank, and were forced to bend it back and hastily entrench it wherever it happened to be.

Not only was the Russian army on the twenty-sixth defended by weak, unfinished entrenchments, but the disadvantage of that position was increased by the fact that the Russian commanders—not having fully grasped what had happened, namely the loss of our position on the left flank and the shifting of the entire battlefield from right to left—maintained their extended position from the village of Novoe to Utitsa, and consequently had to shift their forces from right to left during the battle. So throughout the entire battle, the Russians opposed the entire French army launched against our left flank with only half as many men. (Poniatowski's action against Utitsa and Uvarov's on the right flank against the French were separate actions from the main battle.) So the battle of Borodino was not fought at all as it has been described (in an effort to conceal the commanders' mistakes, even at the cost of diminishing the glory due to the Russian army and people). The battle of Borodino was not fought on a pre-chosen, entrenched position with forces only slightly weaker than the enemy's. Rather, as a result of the loss of the Shevardino Redoubt, the Russians fought the battle of Borodino on an open and almost unfortified position, with forces only half as numerous as the French—that is, under conditions in which it was not merely unthinkable to fight for ten hours and achieve an indecisive result, but unthinkable to keep an army from complete collapse and rout.
